title: A Loud Murmur and Thrill in a Young Man / Sternal Edge, Not the Apex

blocks.text: A Loud Murmur and Thrill in a Young Man / Sternal Edge, Not the Apex

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-17 · Physical examination · PACES Station 3, cardiovascular examination · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 minutes (up to 6 minutes examining, then at least 4 minutes of examiner questions) · Guidelines: 2020 ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease (Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645); NICE CG64 Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis (published 17 March 2008; last updated 8 July 2016) · Related AMaC: AMaC Eisenmenger and ASD stations; this one tests a ventricular septal defect with a left-to-right shunt

The patient is a man of 31, a primary school teacher. A murmur has been known since childhood. He is getting more breathless on stairs. Please examine his cardiovascular system to establish the cause.
You may examine for up to 6 minutes. The examiners will then ask you questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A harsh pansystolic murmur with a thrill at the left sternal edge in a well young adult is a ventricular septal defect. The station turns on placing the murmur correctly, not calling it mitral regurgitation, and asking about the shunt and the pulmonary pressure.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates call a pansystolic murmur mitral regurgitation and listen only at the apex. Pass: left sternal edge, thrill, no radiation to the axilla, shunt, pulmonary pressure. Fail: mitral regurgitation, with no cyanosis check.

rows: He is well. Look at his colour, hands and nails, then the pulse and neck before the chest.
"May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable?"
Clean hands; introduce, consent; sit him at 45 degrees; colour; clubbing; pulse; blood pressure; neck veins.
Palpate for the thrill and the heave, then listen at the left sternal edge and the apex.
"I'm going to feel your chest and listen to your heart, then check your lungs and ankles."
Apex; thrill; heave; heart sounds; murmur; axilla; lung bases; liver; ankles; cover him.
Name the lesion, what the shunt does, and the tests that decide closure.
"He has a ventricular septal defect with a left-to-right shunt. He needs echo and pulmonary pressure assessment."
Present in order; diagnosis; complications; echo; catheter; closure; follow-up; thank him.
Starts without consent; presses hard on the chest; leaves him exposed.
Cleans hands, introduces self, consents, asks about pain, sits him at 45 degrees, covers him afterwards.
Also offers a chaperone and stops if he is breathless.
Disorganised; omits the thrill, the sternal edge or the lung bases.
Looks at hands, colour and neck veins, palpates apex, thrill and heave, listens at the sternal edge, apex and axilla, then bases and ankles.
Also checks the pulse volume, listens in the neck and feels for the liver edge.
Reports cyanosis, clubbing or a diastolic murmur that are absent.
Finds a pansystolic murmur and thrill at the left sternal edge, no radiation to the axilla, normal second sound, and no cyanosis or clubbing.
Also finds a mildly displaced apex, a soft third sound and clear lung bases.
Calls it mitral regurgitation or aortic stenosis.
Ventricular septal defect with a left-to-right shunt.
Also separates it from tricuspid regurgitation and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, with the reason for each.
Names pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome, left heart volume overload, arrhythmia and endocarditis; asks for ECG, echo and chest X-ray.
Also asks for the shunt ratio and a calculated pulmonary vascular resistance, by echo and catheter.
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): calls a cyanosed or deteriorating patient well. Also sends him away without assessing pulmonary pressure.

Says closure is a congenital heart team decision, considered for a significant shunt (ratio above 1.5 to 1) with left heart volume overload, no desaturation and low pulmonary vascular resistance, and follow-up continues.

Also gives the resistance bands for closure (ESC 2020: Class I below 3 Wood units, IIa for 3 to 5), says resistance of 5 or more needs an expert centre decision, and that Eisenmenger physiology or desaturation on exercise is against closure.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type.

Findings, released as each step is done: well; respiratory rate 14; pulse 76 regular; blood pressure 118/72; SpO2 98% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. No clubbing, no cyanosis. Jugular venous pressure not raised. Apex mildly displaced. A thrill at the left sternal edge. Pansystolic murmur loudest at the lower left sternal edge, not radiating to the axilla. Second heart sound normal. Soft third sound. Lung bases clear. No oedema. Liver not palpable.

Question ladder: 1. What do you find? (B) 2. Diagnosis? (D) 3. Complications? (E) 4. Which tests? (E) 5. When is closure considered? (E) A congenital team decision: a significant shunt with left heart overload, no desaturation, and low resistance.

Curveballs: He asks if he can play football: advice from the congenital team. He becomes cyanosed on exertion: suggests a reversed shunt, urgent referral. He asks about the dentist: good dental hygiene and regular checks matter; routine antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work is not recommended for this lesion (NICE CG64).
Cleans hands, introduces self, gains consent and asks about pain (G)
Checks colour, hands, pulse and neck veins (A)
Palpates for the thrill and heave (A)
Finds a pansystolic murmur and thrill at the left sternal edge (B)
States no cyanosis, no clubbing and no radiation to the axilla (B)
Names ventricular septal defect, not mitral regurgitation (D)
Lists pulmonary hypertension, Eisenmenger syndrome and endocarditis (E)
Requests ECG, echo and pulmonary vascular resistance (E)
Says closure is a congenital team decision based on shunt ratio, left heart overload and resistance (E)
Covers him, cleans hands and thanks him (G)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Lie flat. [R1 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Listens at the apex only.) [R2 Fail] Mitral regurgitation, with cyanosis. [R3 Fail] Mitral regurgitation. [R4 Fail]
EXAMINER: Complications and tests?
CANDIDATE: Heart failure. [R5 Fail] He is well, so nothing more is needed. [R6 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): the examiner sees a red flag, because pulmonary pressure decides treatment, and a missed reversal of the shunt is dangerous. No consent, the sternal edge skipped, and the lesion misnamed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your heart? Does anything hurt? Is this angle comfortable? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, colour, pulse, neck veins; thrill and heave; sternal edge, apex and axilla; bases and ankles.) [R2 Pass]
CANDIDATE: He has a thrill and a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge that does not radiate to the axilla, with no cyanosis or clubbing. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands.) Thank you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: A ventricular septal defect. [R4 Pass]
EXAMINER: Complications and tests?
CANDIDATE: Pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome, arrhythmia, endocarditis. ECG, echo and a chest X-ray. [R5 Pass]
EXAMINER: Management?

CANDIDATE: The congenital heart team considers closure for a significant shunt, a ratio above 1.5 to 1 with left heart volume overload, no desaturation and low pulmonary resistance, with lifelong follow-up. [R6 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and complete. Did not name the differential, the resistance bands or the expert-centre decision.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'll stop if you're breathless. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: (Hands, colour, pulse volume, neck veins; thrill; sternal edge, apex, axilla, neck; bases; liver; ankles.) [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: Thrill, pansystolic murmur at the sternal edge, mildly displaced apex, soft third sound, normal second sound, no cyanosis. [R3 High]
EXAMINER: Diagnosis?
CANDIDATE: A ventricular septal defect, not tricuspid regurgitation or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, because of the thrill and no radiation. [R4 High]
EXAMINER: Tests?
CANDIDATE: ECG, echo, chest X-ray; the shunt ratio and pulmonary vascular resistance by echo and catheter. Endocarditis and Eisenmenger syndrome are the risks. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: Management?

CANDIDATE: The congenital team considers closure for a shunt above 1.5 to 1 with left heart volume overload and no desaturation; in ESC 2020 closure is Class I with left heart volume overload and resistance below 3 Wood units, Class IIa at 3 to 5, and Class IIb at 5 or more (an individual decision in an expert centre); with Eisenmenger physiology or desaturation on exercise it is not recommended. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: (Covers him, cleans hands, thanks him.) [R1 High]
Examiner note: Added the chaperone, the differential, the shunt ratio and resistance, endocarditis, and the closure bands.
R2: Listening only at the apex. A ventricular septal defect is loudest at the lower left sternal edge.
R4: Calling it mitral regurgitation. That murmur radiates to the axilla and has no thrill at the sternal edge.
R5: Naming heart failure alone. Pulmonary hypertension decides whether closure is safe.
R6: Calling him well and stopping. Pulmonary resistance must be assessed before any closure decision.
"May I move my stethoscope to the left sternal edge and feel for a thrill?"
"The murmur doesn't radiate to the axilla, so I'd say a ventricular septal defect."
"May I summarise what I found and give my diagnosis?"

Ventricular septal defect: harsh pansystolic murmur and thrill at the lower left sternal edge; a left-to-right shunt can overload the left heart, and a rising pulmonary pressure can reverse it (Eisenmenger syndrome).

ESC 2020: closure is a congenital heart team decision. Closure is recommended regardless of symptoms (Class I) when there is left ventricular volume overload and no pulmonary hypertension (pulmonary vascular resistance below 3 Wood units). With resistance of 3 to 5 Wood units, closure should be considered if there is still a significant left-to-right shunt (ratio above 1.5 to 1; Class IIa); at 5 Wood units or more it may be considered with the same shunt, but needs a careful individual decision in an expert centre (Class IIb). Closure is not recommended with Eisenmenger physiology, or with severe pulmonary hypertension (5 Wood units or more) and desaturation on exercise (Class III). Resistance alone does not decide: the team also weighs left heart volume overload, symptoms, desaturation and any Eisenmenger physiology, where closure is not appropriate.

Endocarditis is a recognised risk of a ventricular septal defect: stress dental hygiene; routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended (NICE CG64). Lifelong follow-up at a congenital heart disease service.
THINK: Sternal-edge pansystolic murmur and thrill: VSD.
SAY: "A hole between the ventricles."
DO: Palpate the thrill; listen at the sternal edge.
NUMBERS: Left heart volume overload with resistance below 3 Wood units: Class I; 3 to 5 with shunt above 1.5 to 1: Class IIa (ESC 2020); team decision.
TRAP: Mitral regurgitation; apex only.
FINISH: Echo, resistance, closure decision, follow-up.

2020 ESC Guidelines for the management of adult congenital heart disease. Eur Heart J 2021;42:563-645. https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/42/6/563/5898937 Supports: Closure of ventricular septal defect by shunt ratio and pulmonary vascular resistance class (below 3, 3 to 5, above 5 Wood units), as summarised in the ACC key points, https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2020/08/29/13/17/2020-esc-guidelines-for-adult-chd-esc-2020.

NICE CG64 Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis (published 17 March 2008; last updated 8 July 2016). https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg64 Supports: antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended routinely for dental procedures in structural heart disease.
